summary:
Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the ruling as a landmark for gender-identity discrimination. A person excluded from a service on the basis of gender identity has a federal remedy, and damages have been awarded in practice.

Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 carries the same grounds and takes effect on 30 June 2026. Coverage outside that federal layer is uneven: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria reach sexual orientation only, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland include gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. No charging or prosecution data for any of these provisions appears in the sources reviewed.

An ANROWS research briefing on threats to trans and gender-diverse rights in Australia records organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over facilities and over access to official records, and rights-rollback pressure. Facilities and records access are the documented points of friction.

Health care: Medicare covers many major sex reassignment surgeries, but the gap between the benefit and the surgeon's fee can run to thousands of dollars, and private hospital policies or insurers typically impose a waiting period of about 12 months before claims for surgery. Since November 2017 a trans child can obtain puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where the child, parents and doctors agree; blockers are treated as a first, reversible stage from around age 10 and hormone therapy as a second, irreversible stage usually from 16, with surgery generally unavailable before 18.

Queensland paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services in January 2025, exempting existing patients; the state's Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025; a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews; a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible but called for more long-term research.

Same-sex marriage was legalised on 9 December 2017 by the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017, following a postal survey in which 61.6 per cent voted Yes. Marriages validly entered overseas are automatically recognised, and married couples can no longer be barred from divorcing.

Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009, through reforms amending 85 federal laws spanning taxation, superannuation, health, social security, aged care, child support, immigration, citizenship and veterans' affairs; Centrelink recognised same-sex de facto partners from 1 July 2009. States and territories have provided relationship recognition since 2003: civil partnerships in the ACT and Queensland, registered partnerships in New South Wales, Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, while Western Australia and the Northern Territory have no such scheme, so couples there often need judicial approval to prove a de facto relationship. De facto partners face longer eligibility periods and a heavier burden of proof than married couples, with requirements differing between Centrelink, migration and family law; this can impede arranging a partner's funeral and is poorly understood by some government departments.

Age of consent is 16 in every jurisdiction for all sexual acts, except Tasmania and South Australia, where it is 17. Queensland was the last to equalise, in 2016, lowering anal intercourse from 18 to 16.

Sex designations on official documents have been a documented point of friction: a 2003 Queensland parliamentary research brief recorded trans people's difficulties changing the sex designation on passports, licences and birth certificates, high rates of job loss around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.
tangentialFactors:
Public expression is both visible and contested. Sydney hosts an annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras and has been named among the most gay-friendly cities in the world, while the ANROWS briefing documents organised campaigns against trans inclusion.

The country's criminal law no longer prohibits same-sex conduct. The prohibitions inherited from British law, which carried the death penalty in Victoria until 1949, were repealed jurisdiction by jurisdiction, and the age of consent was equalised across all jurisdictions by 2016.

Intersex status is a separate protected attribute under the February 2025 hate-crime law, listed alongside gender identity. Intersex organisations argue that intersex is not a gender identity and warn against folding intersex into sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity frameworks, recommending the broader SOGIESC formulation; the distinction shapes how Australian gender-diversity protections are scoped.
localsOnly:
Queensland's 2009 corrective-services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight was replaced through the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023. The inspector's August 2023 standards for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Staff retain discretion at admission, and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process.

From 1 August 2013 religious aged care providers receiving Commonwealth funding cannot exclude people on the basis of LGBTI status or same-sex relationships.

Religious educational institutions may still discriminate against LGBT students and teachers under sections 37 and 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984. Discrimination against LGBT students is barred in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, and Tasmania carries the fewest exemptions of any jurisdiction. The Safe Schools Coalition Australia began in Victoria in 2010 and ran nationally from 2014 until the Turnbull government restricted it to high schools, removed role plays and required parental consent, and it lost federal funding after mid-2017; Victoria, the ACT and South Australia now fund it themselves.

From April 2025 Medicare IVF rebates were extended to single individuals and same-sex couples; surrogacy is not covered. The 2021 Census counted 13,554 children (17.3 per cent) in same-sex couple families, up from 6,915 (14.8 per cent) in 2016.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Queensland Human Rights Commission item on strengthened discrimination protections for gender-diverse people under Queensland's anti-discrimination reform could not be retrieved (the page returned a 404 at research time), so the reform's current status is unresolved here. A New South Wales Parliament bill document likewise could not be retrieved and no claim is drawn from it.

Current requirements for changing gender markers on federal passports and on state and territory birth certificates are not covered by the sources reviewed; the documents material available dates from 2003.

No charging, prosecution or sentencing data for the February 2025 federal hate-crime provisions or for the state and territory vilification laws appears in the sources.

The Queensland ministerial directive restricting under-18 prescriptions was subject to reviews and to a legal challenge filed in December 2025; the outcome is not known.

Custody placement standards are sourced only for Queensland, and no comparable material for other jurisdictions was found. How Australian law classifies a trans person's marriage or partnership where recorded sex status differs between jurisdictions is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
